question.text: The binomial option pricing model differs from Black-Scholes primarily because:

answer.text: It uses a discrete tree-based approach with multiple time steps
It requires fewer inputs than Black-Scholes
It can only price European options
It does not account for volatility

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook describes the binomial model as using a binomial tree with equally spaced time steps and iterative up/down movements, whereas Black-Scholes is a non-iterative closed-form formula that takes the five pricing inputs (spot/futures price, strike, time, risk-free rate, volatility). The Trap: Binomial does not require fewer inputs; it does take volatility into account; and being "European only" is not the distinguishing feature -- the tree-based, iterative time-step structure is. Note: The key contrast emphasised in the workbook is tree-based iterative time steps versus the Black-Scholes single-step formula.
